597142:
Board-Style Case Set: A teenager with new cavities

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 19-year-old college student has four new early (incipient) carious lesions. He sips sweetened soda through the afternoon and keeps hard candy in his mouth while he studies. The hygienist suggests sugar-free gum sweetened with xylitol.

Case Set Question 8.1

Sucrose, the sugar in soda and candy, is a disaccharide made of

  1. glucose + galactose
  2. glucose + fructose
  3. glucose + glucose
  4. fructose + galactose
Answer
B. Sucrose is glucose joined to fructose; lactose is glucose + galactose, and maltose is two glucose units (Section 8.6).

Case Set Question 8.2

Plaque bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans ferment sugars into a product that lowers plaque pH and dissolves enamel. That product is

  1. lactic acid
  2. ethanol
  3. glycogen
  4. cellulose
Answer
A. Bacterial fermentation of sugar produces lactic acid; below about pH 5.5 enamel starts to demineralize.

Case Set Question 8.3

Xylitol is recommended because it

  1. is a sugar alcohol that cavity-causing bacteria cannot ferment to acid
  2. is a polysaccharide too large to be digested
  3. is an amine that neutralizes plaque acid
  4. is a reducing sugar that raises plaque pH
Answer
A. Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol (polyol). It tastes sweet, but S. mutans cannot ferment it, so no acid forms.

597151:
Board-Style Case Set: A patient on a statin

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 58-year-old man with generalized periodontitis lists atorvastatin on his health history for high cholesterol. His last lipid panel showed LDL 165 mg/dL and triglycerides 210 mg/dL. Before scaling, the hygienist gives a local anesthetic injection.

Case Set Question 9.1

A triglyceride is

  1. glycerol joined by three ester bonds to three fatty acids
  2. three glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds
  3. a steroid with four fused rings
  4. a phospholipid with a choline head
Answer
A. Triglycerides (triacylglycerols) are triesters of glycerol (Section 9.2).

Case Set Question 9.2

Cholesterol is classified as a

  1. steroid, a non-hydrolyzable lipid
  2. triglyceride
  3. glycerophospholipid
  4. fatty acid
Answer
A. Cholesterol has the four fused rings of a steroid and contains no ester to hydrolyze (Section 9.6).

Case Set Question 9.3

A local anesthetic must cross the nerve cell membrane before it can work. Which form of the anesthetic crosses the phospholipid bilayer?

  1. The uncharged (free base) form, because the interior of the bilayer is nonpolar
  2. The charged (ammonium) form, because the bilayer interior is polar
  3. Either form equally
  4. Neither; it enters through the cell’s glucose transporters
Answer
A. Only the uncharged form dissolves in the nonpolar tails of the bilayer (Section 9.5). Inflamed, acidic tissue shifts more drug to the charged form, which is why anesthesia works less well there.

597165:
Board-Style Case Set: A patient with sickle cell disease

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease arrives for a routine cleaning. She reports occasional pain crises and is fatigued. After the appointment, the instruments are cleaned and sterilized in an autoclave.

Case Set Question 10.1

Sickle cell disease is caused by a change in which level of hemoglobin structure?

  1. primary
  2. secondary
  3. tertiary
  4. quaternary
Answer
A. One amino acid in the β chain is replaced (glutamate → valine): a change in the amino acid sequence, the primary structure. The change in shape and clumping follows from it (Section 10.6).

Case Set Question 10.2

In sickle hemoglobin, glutamate is replaced by valine. This swaps

  1. an acidic, charged side chain for a nonpolar one
  2. a nonpolar side chain for an acidic one
  3. a basic side chain for an acidic one
  4. a polar neutral side chain for a basic one
Answer
A. Glutamate has a COO− side chain; valine’s side chain is a nonpolar hydrocarbon. The nonpolar patch makes hemoglobin molecules stick together.

Case Set Question 10.3

An autoclave kills bacteria on instruments mainly because heat

  1. denatures their proteins by disrupting secondary and tertiary structure
  2. hydrolyzes every peptide bond into free amino acids
  3. oxidizes their DNA into CO2
  4. converts their lipids into soap
Answer
A. Denaturation disrupts the weak interactions that hold a protein’s shape; the peptide bonds (primary structure) survive (Section 10.10).

597174:
Board-Style Case Set: Bleeding gums and a blood thinner

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 70-year-old man with a limited diet has swollen gums that bleed easily, and his health history lists warfarin for atrial fibrillation. The hygienist notes a possible vitamin C deficiency and plans for extra bleeding.

Case Set Question 11.1

Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) causes fragile, bleeding gums because vitamin C is needed

  1. as a cofactor for the enzyme that hydroxylates proline in collagen
  2. as the precursor of the clotting factors
  3. to make the phospholipids of gum tissue
  4. to break down fibrin clots
Answer
A. Without vitamin C, collagen is not properly hydroxylated and the connective tissue of the gums weakens (Section 11.5).

Case Set Question 11.2

Vitamin C is a

  1. water-soluble vitamin with little storage in the body
  2. fat-soluble vitamin stored in the liver
  3. coenzyme form of vitamin K
  4. steroid hormone
Answer
A. Vitamin C and the B vitamins are water-soluble and must be eaten regularly; vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

Case Set Question 11.3

Warfarin lowers clotting by interfering with vitamin K. Vitamin K is

  1. a fat-soluble vitamin needed to activate several clotting factors
  2. a water-soluble vitamin needed for collagen
  3. a B vitamin that carries acetyl groups
  4. the enzyme that dissolves clots
Answer
A. Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is required to activate clotting factors; warfarin blocks its recycling, so the patient bleeds more easily.

597185:
Board-Style Case Set: A cold sore on the day of the appointment

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 32-year-old woman arrives for her recall appointment with an active, crusting cold sore (herpes labialis) on her lower lip. She says her physician prescribed acyclovir. Radiographs are due today.

Case Set Question 12.1

The best plan for elective treatment is to

  1. reschedule until the lesion has healed
  2. proceed, using extra lip lubricant
  3. proceed, since herpes is not spread by contact
  4. apply acyclovir and continue immediately
Answer
A. An active lesion is contagious and can be spread to other sites; elective care waits until it heals (Section 12.7).

Case Set Question 12.2

Acyclovir stops the virus from

  1. replicating its DNA, because the drug has no 3′-OH and terminates the chain
  2. making proteins at the ribosome
  3. attaching to the cell membrane
  4. transcribing RNA into DNA
Answer
A. Viral DNA polymerase adds acyclovir to the growing strand, but without a 3′-OH the next phosphodiester bond cannot form.

Case Set Question 12.3

Dental radiographs follow the ALARA principle because ionizing radiation

  1. can damage DNA and cause mutations
  2. denatures salivary enzymes
  3. hydrolyzes the enamel
  4. oxidizes fatty acids in the gums
Answer
A. Ionizing radiation can break DNA strands and alter bases, so exposure is kept as low as reasonably achievable (Section 12.6).

597199:
Board-Style Case Set: Shaky and sweaty in the chair

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 27-year-old man with type 1 diabetes took his morning insulin but skipped breakfast to make an early appointment. Twenty minutes in, he becomes shaky, sweaty and confused, but he is conscious and can swallow.

Case Set Question 13.1

His symptoms most likely indicate

  1. hypoglycemia (low blood glucose)
  2. hyperglycemia (high blood glucose)
  3. diabetic ketoacidosis
  4. an allergic reaction to latex
Answer
A. Insulin without food drives blood glucose down; shakiness, sweating and confusion are classic signs of hypoglycemia (Section 13.7).

Case Set Question 13.2

A glucose gel or fruit juice raises his blood glucose quickly because

  1. glucose is a monosaccharide that is absorbed without digestion
  2. glucose must first be hydrolyzed by salivary amylase
  3. juice contains glycogen
  4. sugar is converted to fat first
Answer
A. Monosaccharides need no digestion and enter the blood directly; starch must first be hydrolyzed (Section 13.3).

Case Set Question 13.3

Which hormone raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown in the liver?

  1. glucagon
  2. insulin
  3. aldosterone
  4. oxytocin
Answer
A. Glucagon (and epinephrine) trigger glycogenolysis; insulin does the opposite (Section 13.8).

Case set by Daniel Kwasniewski, Fresno City College, CC BY 4.0.
597206:
Board-Style Case Set: A tired patient with anemia

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 45-year-old woman with iron-deficiency anemia says she is tired all the time and gets short of breath on the stairs. Her hemoglobin is low, so less oxygen reaches her tissues.

Case Set Question 14.1

In the electron transport chain, the final electron acceptor is

  1. O2, which is reduced to water
  2. NAD+
  3. CO2
  4. glucose
Answer
A. Complex IV passes electrons to O2, making H2O; without enough O2 the chain slows (Section 14.4).

Case Set Question 14.2

Most of the ATP from one glucose molecule is made by

  1. oxidative phosphorylation through ATP synthase
  2. glycolysis
  3. substrate-level phosphorylation in the citric acid cycle
  4. digestion
Answer
A. About 26–28 of the roughly 30–32 ATP per glucose come from oxidative phosphorylation (Section 14.5).

Case Set Question 14.3

When tissues are short of oxygen, cells keep glycolysis running by converting pyruvate to

  1. lactate
  2. acetyl CoA
  3. oxaloacetate
  4. urea
Answer
A. Reducing pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ for glycolysis when the chain cannot (Section 13.5).

597219:
Board-Style Case Set: Fruity breath

Health-care licensing exams such as the National Board Dental Hygiene Examination use case sets: a short patient scenario followed by several questions. Read the case, then answer each question.

The case

A 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes has missed several insulin doses. At the appointment the hygienist notices a fruity odor on his breath and rapid, deep breathing, and refers him for immediate medical care.

Case Set Question 15.1

The fruity odor comes from

  1. acetone, a ketone body
  2. ethanol
  3. lactic acid
  4. ammonia
Answer
A. Acetone forms from acetoacetate and is exhaled (Section 15.7).

Case Set Question 15.2

Ketone bodies are made in the liver from

  1. acetyl CoA produced by fatty acid oxidation
  2. glucose produced by gluconeogenesis
  3. urea from the urea cycle
  4. amino acids released by digestion
Answer
A. Without insulin, fat breakdown floods the liver with acetyl CoA, which is turned into ketone bodies (Sections 15.3 and 15.7).

Case Set Question 15.3

The rapid, deep breathing is the body’s attempt to correct

  1. metabolic acidosis caused by the acidic ketone bodies
  2. alkalosis caused by excess bicarbonate
  3. low blood glucose
  4. high blood ammonia
Answer
A. Acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid lower blood pH; breathing off CO2 partly compensates.
